details:
**The Second Sex (Simone de Beauvoir)**
The 1949 existentialist work by the French philosopher Simone de Beauvoir, a founding text of modern feminism. It appears in nearly every question on women, usually as the giveaway.

**"One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman"**
The most famous line of The Second Sex. Beauvoir means that "woman" is not a fixed natural essence but a role that society shapes and imposes on people.

**Woman as the "Other"**
Beauvoir argues that society defines man as the default subject and defines woman only in relation to him, as the "Other." Women are thus treated as secondary, or as a "privileged Other," instead of as full subjects in their own right.

**The Subjection of Women (John Stuart Mill)**
An 1869 utilitarian essay by John Stuart Mill, written with ideas developed with his wife Harriet Taylor, who had died before it was published. It compares women's legal position in marriage to slavery and argues that women should be free to compete for any job, a "free market" for their abilities.

**"Facts and Myths" and "Lived Experience"**
The titles of the two volumes of The Second Sex. The first looks at what biology, psychoanalysis, history, and myth say about women, including criticism of the Napoleonic Code. The second describes women's lives from childhood through marriage and old age.

**Immanence and transcendence**
Beauvoir's existentialist terms. Men are allowed transcendence, meaning free, creative action that shapes the future, while women are confined to immanence, meaning repetitive, passive life such as housework.

**"Situations" and "Justifications"**
Sections of the second volume of The Second Sex. Beauvoir discusses women's social "situation" and then criticizes the "justifications" some women use to cope with it, in chapters on the narcissist, the woman in love, and the mystic.

**The Feminine Mystique and "the problem that has no name"**
Betty Friedan's 1963 book, which launched second-wave feminism in the United States. Friedan describes the "problem that has no name," the unhappiness of suburban housewives who asked themselves "Is this all?" She also argued that women were kept from rising up Maslow's hierarchy of needs toward self-actualization. Friedan later co-founded the National Organization for Women (NOW).

**A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (Mary Wollstonecraft)**
Mary Wollstonecraft's 1792 work arguing that women deserve the same education as men and should be companions to their husbands, not ornaments. It responds to Talleyrand's plan for French education and criticizes conduct books by James Fordyce and John Gregory, as well as Rousseau's views on women's education in Emile. Her husband William Godwin later wrote a memoir of her.

**The Female Eunuch (Germaine Greer)**
A 1970 book by the Australian feminist Germaine Greer. She argues that consumer society has cut women off from their own sexuality and energy, turning them into "eunuchs."

**"Outsider-within" (Patricia Hill Collins)**
A concept from Patricia Hill Collins, author of Black Feminist Thought. It describes Black women who work inside dominant institutions, such as domestic workers in white homes, but are never fully accepted there, giving them a special view of those institutions.

**Woman in the Nineteenth Century (Margaret Fuller)**
An 1845 book by the American Transcendentalist Margaret Fuller, one of the first major feminist works in the United States. It argues that women's progress in America has been held back by prejudices inherited from Europe.

**Schopenhauer's "On Women"**
An essay by the German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer, known for its hostility to women. He claims that the shape of women's bodies shows they are not meant for great mental or physical labor.

**"Did Women Have a Renaissance?" (Joan Kelly)**
A 1977 essay by the historian Joan Kelly. She argues that women did not have a Renaissance during the period of the Renaissance, because the changes of that era actually reduced the freedom of upper-class women.

**Feminist Theory: From Margin to Center (bell hooks)**
A 1984 book by bell hooks, which criticizes mainstream feminism for focusing on white, middle-class women. It argues that feminism must include the experiences of Black and working-class women.
